previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, COPD, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease was admitted for acute shortness of breath and chest pain. His symptoms were attributed to acute on chronic systolic heart failure with fluid overload, exacerbated by underlying restrictive lung disease and COPD. He was treated with IV diuretics, leading to improved oxygenation and resolution of congestion. His kidney function, initially impaired due to poor perfusion, improved with diuresis. The chest pain was deemed non-ischemic based on stable troponin and lack of EKG changes. He was discharged home on increased torsemide, with instructions to monitor weight, adhere to a low-sodium diet, continue insulin and cardiac medications, and follow up with counseling for substance use and medication adherence.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old male with non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (EF 
20%), COPD, polysubstance abuse, cocaine-induced pulmonary 
fibrosis, previous episodes of pneumonia, multiple 
hospitalizations for COPD/CHF now admitted with dypsnea and 
hypoxemia, s/p syncope likely secondary to hypoxemia.  He did 
well, was weaned off oxygen and discharged home in stable 
condition.
  
# DYSPNEA: Etiology is likely multifactorial secondary to COPD 
exacerbation and mild CHF exacerbation, in the setting of 
chronic interstitial lung disease secondary to cocaine abuse. 
His dry weight at last discharge on ___ was 85 kg and his 
admission weight was over 88 kg. He received a prednisone 40 mg 
daily burst, azithromycin x 5 days, albuterol and ipratropium 
nebulizers standing. He was given furosemide IV x 1 in the ED 
but then continued on home torsemide 80 mg daily for diuresis. 
On presentation, he was on 100% non-rebreather briefly, weaned 
down to 4L NC by the time of admission, and was satting mid-90s 
on room air by the time of discharge. He was also at his dry 
weight of 85 kg on the day of discharge. He should continue his 
home inhalers for COPD and home torsemide 80 mg daily for CHF. 

# SYNCOPE: Etiology of reported syncope prior to admission is 
likely dyspnea and hypoxemia rather than cardiac as patient 
improved with supplemental oxygen. Cardiac enzymes and ECG were 
negative for acute coronary syndrome. On admission, the patient 
was monitored on telemetry for the first 2 days of admission, 
but given no telemetry events and suspicion of cardiac 
dysrhythmias low, he was taken off telemetry. He had no 
pre-syncopal or syncopal events while in house. He remained 
completely hemodynamically stable while inpatient.

# ACUTE ON CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE: On presentation, the 
patient's creatinine was 2.1 from baseline 1.2-1.5, likely 
pre-renal from hypovolemia and possible cardiorenal syndrome.  
Home losartan was held. With diuresis using home torsemide 80mg 
PO daily, creatinine improved to 1.6 on discharge. The patient 
should have creatinine trended by his PCP and can discuss 
restarting losartan with his PCP. He should avoid nephrotoxins 
and NSAIDs.

# TROPONINEMIA/CHF: On presentation, troponin was slightly 
elevated, but CK-MB was within normal limits.  Etiology was most 
likely acute on chronic heart failure given physical exam and 
unchanged ECG. He is not on a beta-blocker due to ongoing 
cocaine use and not on spironolactone due to non-compliance. His 
clinical status improved on his home torsemide 80 mg PO daily. 
Although he states that he faithfully takes his medications at 
home, he also told us that he does not have any money for 
refills. Therefore, it is unclear if he is compliant with his 
home torsemide. On discharge, the patient was diuresed >3 kg and 
back to dry weight of 85 kg. He was continued on his home 
aspirin in-house, but atorvastatin was stopped as the patient 
complained of muscle cramps.  He can discuss with his PCP 
___ to restart atorvastatin.

# MUSCLE CRAMPS: The patient had a few episodes of muscle cramps 
in his extremities and his right side that caused him 
significant pain and anxiety.  These improved with hot packs.  
He also received cyclobenzaprine 10 mg x 1, which helped his 
cramps.  Electrolytes including Ca, Mg, Phos were normal during 
his hospital stay. CK was elevated at 424 but this may be normal 
given his ethnic background. Home atorvastatin 20 mg daily was 
stopped and he should discuss with his PCP when or if to restart 
this medication.  

# DYSURIA: On review of systems on admission, the patient 
endorsed dysuria, foul smelling urine, and urinary frequency.  
UA and Urine culture were checked but negative. Chlamydia and 
gonorrhea testing was sent and still pending on discharge. On 
discharge, the patient had no urinary symptoms.

# ANXIETY AND SOCIAL ISSUES: Per discussion with the PCP, 
patient does not have resources to refill his prescriptions and 
he was also having significant anxiety but had failed to 
successfully have psych followup. The patient was seen by PACT 
inpatient, and they will follow up with him ___ regarding 
getting his copay covered via ___ Caremark. The patient knows to 
keep his scheduled PCP appointment on ___ to follow up about 
these issues. He was given lorazepam 0.5 mg QHS:PRN anxiety and 
will be discharged with prescription for 3 pills of lorazepam 
until his PCP ___.

# DIABETES: The patient was persistently hyperglycemic to finger 
sticks > 300s-400s while on prednisone burst despite increasing 
Lantus doses. Finger sticks improved with discontinuation of 
prednisone. On discharge, he should be continued on his home 
insulin regimen.

# LEUKOCYTOSIS: WBC trended up to 12.2 from 8.5 on admission. 
This uptrend correlated with timing of prednisone burst, so 
likely secondary to steroids. The patient had no other 
localizing signs of infection other than cough that was present 
prior to admission and some dysuria, however UA/urine culture 
was negative and CXR was negative for pneumonia.  WBC was 
trending down to 11.4 on discharge. PCP can follow up WBC count 
to ensure resolution of leukocytosis.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Mr. ___,

You were admitted to the hospital for difficulty breathing. This 
was due to too much fluid in your lungs from your heart 
condition (congestive heart failure) and some worsening of your 
COPD. You were given Torsemide, which helps remove the fluid 
from your lungs. You were also given a short course of steroids 
and antibiotics for your COPD. You received nebulizer 
treatments. You improved with these medications and no longer 
required oxygen before you were discharged.

Please weigh yourself every morning and call your doctor if 
weight goes up more than 3 lbs. This means that too much fluid 
is accumulating in your lungs again.

You should keep your appointment with your PCP ___ on 
___. At that appointment, you can discuss your 
Ativan prescription, money for your medications, and make sure 
that your breathing is still good.  

It was a pleasure to take care you during your hospital stay. We 
wish you a speedy recovery.
Your ___ Team
